Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) reduce the synthesis of vasodilating renal prostaglandins, which can disrupt fluid homeostasis and potentially diminish the efficacy of antihypertensive medications. Close monitoring is advised. 2. Aspirin combined with citric acid and sodium bicarbonate increases serum potassium levels, while furosemide decreases serum potassium. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, so caution is recommended. 3. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate may reduce the effects of furosemide through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This interaction is considered minor, but its clinical significance is unknown. 4. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate can increase the levels or effects of ganciclovir by competing for renal tubular clearance as acidic (anionic) drugs. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is uncertain. 5. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate, as well as garlic, both enhance anticoagulation. Caution and close monitoring are recommended when these agents are used together. 6. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate decrease the levels of gefitinib by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. It is advised to separate the administration of gefitinib and antacids by at least six hours. 7. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate increase serum potassium levels, while gentamicin decreases serum potassium. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, so caution is advised. 8. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate increase the levels of gentamicin by reducing renal clearance. This interaction is minor and primarily occurs in preterm infants. Its clinical significance is unknown. 9. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate, as well as ginger, both enhance anticoagulation. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 10. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate, as well as ginkgo biloba, both enhance anticoagulation. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 11. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate increase the effects of glimepiride through an unknown mechanism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 12. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate increase the effects of glimepiride by competing for plasma protein binding. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is uncertain. 13. Large doses of salicylates can enhance the effects of glimepiride. Close monitoring is advised. 14. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate increase the effects of glipizide through an unknown mechanism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 15. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate increase the effects of glipizide by competing for plasma protein binding. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is uncertain. 16. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate increase the effects of glyburide through an unknown mechanism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 17. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate increase the effects of glyburide by competing for plasma protein binding. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is uncertain. 18. Green tea may enhance the effects of aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate through pharmacodynamic synergism, potentially increasing the risk of bleeding. This interaction is theoretical and attributed to the caffeine content in green tea. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 19. Griseofulvin decreases the levels of aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate through an unknown mechanism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 20. Aspirin, citric acid, and sodium bicarbonate, as well as heparin, both enhance anticoagulation and may increase each other's toxicity. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised.
